answers.flag: The hard requirement 'not keep copies of the users ... in AWS' can be read literally against C, because IAM Identity Center with an Active Directory identity source synchronizes user and group records from AD into its identity store, while B (AD FS SAML to IAM roles) stores no user records in AWS at all; rewording to 'not keep copies of the passwords or maintain a second user directory in AWS' would remove this reading.

case.label: B
case.text: B meets every hard constraint: no domain controllers in AWS, no passwords in AWS, and, read literally, no copies of the users either, since SAML federation to IAM roles keeps no user objects in AWS, whereas Identity Center with AD Connector syncs user and group identity data from AD into the Identity Center identity store. If a candidate treats that sync as 'keeping copies of the users', C fails a requirement and B becomes the only compliant option, and LEAST operational overhead only ranks options that meet the requirements. The stem also does not say whether an AD FS server already exists; if it does, the extra work for B is one identity provider and role set per account, which can be automated with StackSets. Against B: 40 accounts each need an IAM identity provider and roles, and AD FS must be run and maintained, so C is still the better answer under the intended reading. A fails because AWS Managed Microsoft AD runs domain controllers in AWS; D copies users into IAM.
